1.title: Well-Architected, Adoption and Migration
1.text: Welcome to Module two: Well-Architected, Adoption and Migration. This module finishes the first domain of the exam, Cloud Concepts. It covers task statements one point two and one point three: how A W S describes a good design, and how organizations move to the cloud.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Name the six pillars of the A W S Well-Architected Framework, and tell them apart. Say what the A W S Well-Architected Tool is for. Describe the A W S Cloud Adoption Framework and its four business outcomes. Match a situation to one of the seven migration strategies. And know which A W S services help you discover, plan and carry out a migration.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Plans the Move
1.text: Tidewater's board has agreed to move the shop to A W S, and it wants a plan it can trust. The C T O asks how to judge whether the new design is a good one. The C F O asks what outcomes the move should deliver for the business. And the I T lead must decide how to move the web servers, the database, and an old email system. Your job is to choose the frameworks, strategies and services that fit.

1.title: What Is the Well-Architected Framework?
1.text: The A W S Well-Architected Framework is a set of design principles, best practices and questions for building cloud workloads. It is built on six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. A W S compares neglecting a pillar to a weak foundation in a building: the system struggles to meet its goals. Following the pillars helps you build stable and efficient systems, and leaves room for the functional side of the design. The exam asks you to name the pillars and to tell them apart. Exam tip: learn the six names, and one phrase to recognize each.

1.title: The Six Pillars at a Glance
1.text: Here are the six pillars with a short meaning for each. Operational excellence is building correctly, delivering a great customer experience, and running and improving operations. Security is protecting data, systems and assets. Reliability is working correctly and consistently when expected. Performance efficiency is using resources efficiently, and keeping that up as demand changes. Cost optimization is delivering business value at the lowest price point. And sustainability is reducing environmental impact, especially energy use. Exam tip: each pillar answers one question: how to run, protect, keep running, perform, save and sustain.

1.title: Operational Excellence and Security
1.text: Two pillars on this slide. Operational excellence is a commitment to build software correctly while delivering a great customer experience. Its design principles are: perform operations as code, make frequent small reversible changes, refine procedures, anticipate failure, and learn from all failures. Security is the ability to protect data, systems and assets, using cloud technology to improve security. On A W S that includes access management, encryption, logging and threat detection, which Modules three to five cover. Exam tip: operations as code and learning from failure mean operational excellence. Protecting data and systems means security.

1.title: Reliability and Performance Efficiency
1.text: Reliability is the ability of a workload to perform its intended function correctly and consistently when expected. Its principles are: recover automatically from failure, test recovery procedures, scale horizontally, stop guessing capacity, and manage change through automation. Performance efficiency is using cloud resources efficiently to meet performance requirements, and keeping that efficiency as demand and technology change. Its principles are: democratize advanced technologies, go global in minutes, use serverless architectures, experiment more often, and consider mechanical sympathy. Exam tip: recover and test means reliability. Serverless, global and experiments mean performance efficiency.

1.title: Cost Optimization and Sustainability
1.text: Cost optimization is running systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point. Its principles are: implement cloud financial management, adopt a consumption model, measure overall efficiency, stop spending money on undifferentiated heavy lifting, and analyze and attribute expenditure. Sustainability focuses on environmental impacts, especially energy consumption and efficiency. The two often point the same way, because using fewer resources cuts both the bill and the energy. Exam tip: consumption model and heavy lifting mean cost optimization. Energy and environment mean sustainability.

1.title: Telling the Pillars Apart
1.text: Let us practice telling the pillars apart. A question that mentions recovering automatically, testing recovery, or scaling out is about reliability. Operations as code, small reversible changes and learning from failures point to operational excellence. A consumption model, or no undifferentiated heavy lifting, is cost optimization. Serverless, experimenting and going global in minutes belong to performance efficiency. Protecting data, systems and assets is security. And energy use and environmental impact is sustainability. Exam tip: some phrases, such as go global in minutes and stop guessing capacity, appear in more than one place, so read what the question is really asking.

1.title: The AWS Well-Architected Tool
1.text: The A W S Well-Architected Tool is a service in the console for reviewing workloads against best practices. Look at the four steps. You define the workload, answer questions about the pillars, receive an improvement plan, and save milestones. A milestone saves a point in time, so you can track progress. Lenses add best practices for specific kinds of workload, including your own. For cost, check A W S's pricing page. Exam tip: reviewing your design against A W S best practices is the Well-Architected Tool.

1.title: The Cloud Adoption Framework: Purpose and Outcomes
1.text: Now the A W S Cloud Adoption Framework, called the A W S C A F. It draws on A W S experience to help organizations transform digitally. It identifies the capabilities that underpin a successful cloud transformation. You can use it to prioritize opportunities, assess cloud readiness, and evolve your roadmap. It names four business outcomes: reduce business risk, improve environmental, social and governance performance, grow revenue, and increase operational efficiency. Exam tip: the four outcomes to remember are risk, E S G, revenue and efficiency.

1.title: CAF Perspectives and Phases
1.text: The C A F groups its capabilities into six perspectives: Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security and Operations. Business means cloud investments support business outcomes. People covers culture, structure, leadership and workforce. Governance means orchestrating cloud work to maximize benefit and limit risk. It also describes four phases of adoption, shown in the bottom row: Envision, Align, Launch and Scale. Exam tip: perspectives say who and what, and phases say when: envision, align, launch, scale.

1.title: Benefits of Migrating to AWS
1.text: What does migration bring? It moves fixed expense to variable expense, and ends the work of running data centers. It brings the benefits of Module one: speed and agility, elasticity, global reach and economies of scale. The C A F outcomes add lower risk, better E S G performance, revenue growth and operational efficiency. Workloads are also easier to optimize or re-architect once they are running in the cloud. And you choose a strategy for each application, so one project can mix strategies. Exam tip: the benefits of migration repeat the benefits of the cloud.

1.title: Migration Strategies: The Seven Rs
1.text: A W S names seven migration strategies, the seven R s. Look at the picture. Along the top, four strategies run from no change to a full redesign: rehost, relocate, replatform and refactor. Below them are three more: repurchase, retire and retain. You choose a strategy for each application. For large migrations, A W S suggests rehosting, relocating or replatforming first, and modernizing after the move. Refactor is the most complex and costly strategy. Exam tip: read how much change the question allows. None is rehost, some is replatform, a redesign is refactor.

2.title: Rehost, Relocate and Replatform
2.text: Three strategies keep the application mostly as it is. Rehost, also called lift and shift, moves the application without changes, and users keep being served while servers migrate. Relocate moves many servers to the cloud version of the platform, or moves instances to another V P C, Region or account, with no new hardware and no rewrite. Replatform, also called lift, tinker and shift, moves the application and adds some optimization. An example is moving a Microsoft S Q L Server database to Amazon R D S for S Q L Server. Rehosting also makes later optimization easier, because the workload is already on A W S. Exam tip: no changes is rehost, and a few changes for a managed service is replatform.

2.title: Repurchase, Refactor, Retire and Retain
2.text: Four more strategies. Repurchase, also called drop and shop, replaces the application with a different product, often moving from a traditional license to S A A S. Refactor, or re-architect, changes the architecture to use cloud-native features, and it is the most complex and costly strategy. Retire decommissions applications with no business value, such as idle or unused ones. And retain keeps an application where it is for now, for example for data residency, dependencies, or because it was recently upgraded. Exam tip: replace with a product is repurchase. Switch it off is retire. Leave it for now is retain.

2.title: Database Replication With AWS DMS
2.text: A W S Database Migration Service, A W S D M S, migrates relational databases, data warehouses, No S Q L databases and other data stores. Look at the picture. You can do a one-time migration, or replicate ongoing changes to keep the source and the target in sync. That ongoing copying is database replication, and it is the example the exam guide gives. If you are moving to a different engine, convert the schema first, with D M S Schema Conversion or the A W S Schema Conversion Tool, called S C T. D M S is pay as you go, and encrypts data at rest with K M S and in transit with S S L. Exam tip: move a database and keep it in sync is D M S; convert schemas between engines is S C T.

2.title: Migration Services: Discover, Track, Move
2.text: Four services support a migration. A W S Application Discovery Service collects usage and configuration data about on-premises servers. A W S Migration Hub is one place to plan and track migrations. A W S Application Migration Service does lift and shift of servers, with continuous replication, and it is now named A W S Transform M G N. Migration Evaluator builds a data-driven business case with right-sized cost projections. As of the fourth of November, twenty twenty-six, Discovery Service and Migration Hub are closed to new customers, and A W S points to A W S Transform. The exam guide still lists them, so know what each does. Exam tip: find servers, Discovery Service. Track, Migration Hub. Move servers, Application Migration Service. Business case, Migration Evaluator.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Frameworks and Migration
2.text: Here are the look-alike pairs for this module. Reliability or operational excellence: recover and test, or run and learn. Cost optimization or sustainability: the lowest price point, or the lowest environmental impact. Well-Architected Framework or Tool: the guidance, or the review in the console. C A F perspectives or phases: the areas, or the stages in time. Rehost, replatform or refactor: no change, some change, or a redesign. And D M S or S C T: move and replicate data, or convert the schema. Exam tip: name the situation first.

2.title: Design Check: Tidewater's Migration Plan
2.text: Time to design. Look at Tidewater's six needs, and answer each one yourself before I do. To judge whether the new design is a good one, use the Well-Architected Framework and the Tool. To agree the business outcomes, use the C A F: risk, E S G, revenue and efficiency. Moving the web servers exactly as they are is a rehost. Moving the database and keeping it in sync is D M S replication. Replacing the old email system is a repurchase of a S A A S product. And an application nobody uses is a candidate to retire.

2.title: Common Traps: Frameworks and Migration
2.text: Watch for five traps. Pillars are not services: the Well-Architected Framework is guidance, not something you launch. The Tool and the Framework differ: the Tool reviews a workload, and the Framework holds the pillars. Rehost is not replatform: replatform changes something to gain a benefit. Refactor is not the fast option: it is the most complex and costly. And names move: Application Migration Service is now A W S Transform M G N, and older material and questions may use the old name. Exam tip: when a service name looks unfamiliar, think about what the old name did.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. The pillars are operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. To tell them apart: operations as code, protect, recover and test, serverless and experiments, consumption model, and environmental impact. The Tool reviews a workload against best practices, and gives an action plan with milestones. The C A F has six perspectives, four phases, and four outcomes: risk, E S G, revenue and efficiency. The seven R s are retire, retain, rehost, relocate, replatform, repurchase and refactor. And for services: D M S replicates databases, Application Migration Service moves servers, and Migration Evaluator builds the case.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which list names the six pillars of the A W S Well-Architected Framework? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. The other lists mix quality words, service categories or project phases that are not the pillars.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A team keeps its runbooks as code, makes small reversible changes, and reviews every incident to improve its procedures. Which pillar does this describe? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B, operational excellence. Reliability is about recovering and scaling, cost optimization is about price, and performance efficiency is about using resources well.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Tidewater wants its shop to recover from failures without manual work. Which two practices support the reliability pillar? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B: monitoring key indicators and running automation, and replacing one large server with several smaller ones that do not share a failure point. Hand changes, untested recovery and a single large server all raise the risk of failure.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Which statement describes the cost optimization pillar? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: running systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point. The other statements describe security, performance efficiency and sustainability.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Tidewater wants to review its shop against A W S best practices and receive an improvement plan. Which A W S tool fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, the A W S Well-Architected Tool. Artifact provides compliance reports, CloudTrail records account activity, and Inspector scans for vulnerabilities.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which pillar focuses on environmental impacts, especially energy consumption and efficiency? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D, sustainability. The other pillars cover recovering from failure, running operations, and protecting assets.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two are business outcomes that the A W S Cloud Adoption Framework helps organizations pursue? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C: reduced business risk, and increased operational efficiency. The other two outcomes are improved E S G performance and revenue growth. The remaining options are not outcomes the framework describes.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Tidewater moves its web servers to A W S exactly as they are, with no changes to the application. Which migration strategy is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, rehost, also called lift and shift. Refactoring redesigns, repurchasing replaces, and retiring switches off.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. A company replaces its on-premises email system with a vendor's software-as-a-service product. Which migration strategy is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, repurchase, sometimes called drop and shop. Replatforming and relocating keep the same application, and retaining leaves it where it is.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Tidewater must keep its order database running during the move and keep the copy in the cloud in sync until cutover. Which A W S service fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D, A W S Database Migration Service. It migrates databases and can replicate ongoing changes. Athena queries data, Config tracks configuration, and CloudFront delivers content.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. Which statement about migration strategies is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Replatform means moving with some optimization, for example to a managed database service. Refactoring is the most complex and costly strategy, and retiring means decommissioning an application.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all eleven answers. Question one: A. Question two: B. Question three: A and B. Question four: D. Question five: C. Question six: D. Question seven: A and C. Question eight: A. Question nine: C. Question ten: D. Question eleven: B. That completes Module two, and the first domain. Next, Module three opens the Security and Compliance domain with the shared responsibility model.
